meaning: Touched lightly and quickly, again and again, often with a cloth or fingers
trick: DAB = a tiny touch, like dabbing cream on a cut.
examples: Mariam dabbed at her eyes.
She dabbed the cut with cotton.

usage.pattern: dab at something / dab something with something

meaning: Small, light touches or marks; also small amounts of something
trick: DABS of paint = tiny touches of the brush.
examples: He was making dabs with his pencil on the cover of his brief.
She put a few dabs of cream on her face.

usage.pattern: make dabs (with something) / dabs of something

meaning: A short, pointed knife used as a weapon
trick: DAGGER sounds like 'dang-er' - it's a danger in someone's hand.
examples: Rasheed stopped to look at an engraved silver dagger in one shop.
The soldier hid a dagger in his belt.

usage.pattern: a dagger / stab someone with a dagger

meaning: In a small, neat, delicate and careful way
trick: DAINTY + -ly = moving like a tiny ballet dancer.
examples: Mollie came mincing daintily in, chewing at a lump of sugar.
She ate her cake daintily with a small fork.

meaning: Small, pretty and delicate
trick: DAINTY = a tiny DAISY: small and pretty.
examples: Its safe streets were dotted with dainty homes.
She wore a dainty gold necklace.

meaning: Small flowers with white petals and a yellow centre
trick: DAISY - 'day's eye': it opens in the day.
examples: Joy doesn't just sprout out of the ground like daisies and rainbows.
The field was full of daisies in spring.

usage.pattern: pick daisies / a field of daisies

meaning: Something that holds back strong feelings (when it 'breaks', they pour out); also a wall built to hold back water
trick: A DAM holds back a river - and tears too, until it breaks.
examples: As we talked, the dam broke and my fear and sadness came bursting out.
They built a dam across the river.

usage.pattern: the dam breaks / build a dam across something

meaning: Very bad or wicked; deserving punishment from God
trick: DAMN + -able = able to be damned, so truly wicked.
examples: She suspected the act was damnable.
Lying to your mother is a damnable thing.

meaning: Strongly showing that someone is guilty or wrong
trick: A DAMNING lie damns you - it proves you're at fault.
examples: There it was, spoken for the first time, the great, damning lie.
The report was damning for the company.

usage.pattern: a damning + noun / be damning for someone

meaning: Slightly wet, often in an unpleasant way
trick: DAMP = a little wet, like a DAMP towel.
examples: It happened on a damp, overcast day in the spring of 1959.
My clothes are still damp from the rain.

meaning: Moving something gently up and down or from side to side
trick: DANDLE a baby = bounce it gently on your knee.
examples: They were solemnly eyeing me and dandling their heads from side to side.
She sat dandling the baby on her knee.

meaning: To hang or swing loosely
trick: DANGLE - your legs dangle when the chair is too high.
examples: She could do no more than dangle from his arm.
Don't let the wires dangle from the ceiling.

meaning: Hung or swung something loosely
trick: DANGLED - like keys hanging from a hook.
examples: I dangled a pair of fuzzy dice from the rearview mirror.
He dangled his feet in the water.

meaning: Hanging or swinging loosely; also holding out something tempting
trick: DANGLING like a loose earring.
examples: He had a cigarette dangling from his underlip.
The child sat on the wall with her legs dangling.

usage.pattern: something dangling from something / with legs dangling

meaning: Unpleasantly damp, cold and dark
trick: DANK sounds like 'tank' - inside an old water tank: wet and cold.
examples: I made a long descent into the dark, dank forest.
The basement was dank and smelled of mould.

meaning: Neat and stylish in dress and looks (usually a man)
trick: DAPPER = a DAPPER man has a perfect DAP (style).
examples: Their father was a dapper little man.
He looked dapper in his new suit.

meaning: Marked with spots or patches of a different colour or light
trick: DAPPLED - like light through leaves making little dots.
examples: The hot red soil was dappled with vivid green.
We sat in the dappled shade of the trees.

meaning: Used to say you think something is probably true (much like 'I suppose')
trick: I DARE SAY it - I'm bold enough to guess it.
examples: "And I daresay that's why I love you," she added.
I daresay you're tired after the trip.

meaning: Moved suddenly and quickly
trick: A DART flies fast - eyes DARTED fast too.
examples: Her eyes darted from one face to another.
The cat darted under the bed.

meaning: Moving suddenly and quickly from place to place
trick: DARTING like darts flying around.
examples: His gaze was darting back and forth.
Small fish were darting through the water.

usage.pattern: dart back and forth / from something to something

meaning: (Of hopes) destroyed or ruined; also ran quickly
trick: DASHED hopes - dashed (smashed) on the rocks.
examples: There had been six more cycles of hopes raised then dashed.
Her dreams of winning were dashed by the injury.

usage.pattern: someone's hopes are dashed / dash someone's hopes

meaning: Running or moving quickly; also attractive and stylish (of a man)
trick: DASH = sprint (100-metre dash).
examples: Then Laila was dashing around the room.
He was dashing to catch the last bus.

usage.pattern: dash around / to / out of somewhere

meaning: The beginning of something; also the first light of day
trick: DAWN = the start of the day, or the start of anything.
examples: Hostage taking has existed since the dawn of recorded time.
We woke up at dawn to see the sunrise.

usage.pattern: the dawn of something / at dawn

meaning: A state of not thinking clearly, as after a shock
trick: DAZE - like being dazed after a big hit.
examples: I walked around in a daze for years.
After the accident he was in a daze.

meaning: Unable to think clearly, because of shock or a blow
trick: DAZED = stars spinning around your head.
examples: Babi sat looking sheepish and dazed.
He looked dazed after falling off his bike.

meaning: So bright that it hurts your eyes; also very impressive
trick: DAZZLING - so bright it DAZES you.
examples: The sky was so dazzling that I dared not raise my eyes.
The sea was dazzling in the afternoon sun.

meaning: A lazy person who doesn't work or pay what they owe (informal)
trick: DEAD BEAT - his heart beats, but his work is dead.
examples: Jimmy was also a total deadbeat, all talk and no walk.
Her brother is a deadbeat who never pays rent.

meaning: Made weaker or less strong (a feeling, sound or pain)
hindi: सुन्न कर दिया, कमज़ोर कर दिया
trick: DEADENED = made 'dead', so no feeling left.
examples: An eerie quiet expanded and deadened our spirit.
The thick walls deadened the noise.

meaning: So loud that you cannot hear anything else
hindi: कान फाड़ देने वाला, बहुत तेज़
trick: DEAFENING - so loud it could make you DEAF.
examples: Then there was a deafening roar.
The music at the party was deafening.

meaning: Given out (cards); here, given by life or fate
trick: Cards are DEALT - life DEALT you this hand.
examples: Life dealt me a bad hand.
We all get dealt cards we didn't choose.

usage.pattern: be dealt something / deal someone a bad hand

meaning: Likely to cause death
trick: DEATH + INDUCE (bring about) = brings death.
examples: The body has a natural radar for death-inducing situations.
Climbing without ropes felt like a death-inducing risk.

meaning: Broken pieces left after something is destroyed
trick: DEBRIS (day-bree) - what's left after a break.
examples: They pulled from the debris what remained of a sister, a brother.
Workers cleared the debris after the storm.

usage.pattern: clear the debris / pull someone from the debris

meaning: An athlete who competes in the decathlon, an event made of ten sports
trick: DECA = ten (decade = ten years).
examples: Joe was an undersized decathlete in college.
The decathlete ran, jumped and threw in two days.

meaning: The slow process of rotting or breaking down
trick: DECAY - tooth DECAY makes teeth rot.
examples: He suffered through disease, hunger, pain, loneliness, and decay.
Sugar causes tooth decay.

usage.pattern: the decay of something / fall into decay

meaning: A person who has recently died
trick: DECEASED - their life has CEASED.
examples: It was customary for the family of the deceased to sit there.
The deceased was a kind old man.

meaning: Trying to make people believe things that are not true
trick: DECEIT-FULL = full of lies.
examples: Had she been a deceitful wife?
He was deceitful and lied to everyone.

meaning: Polite, honest and respectful behaviour
trick: DECENT person shows DECENCY.
examples: You didn't even have the decency to give me time to say good-bye.
He didn't have the decency to apologise.

usage.pattern: have the decency to do something

meaning: Making someone believe something that is not true
trick: DECEPTION - deceive + -tion.
examples: The economic system promotes such deception.
The magician's trick was clever deception.

meaning: Here, ate all of something quickly (humorous); also destroyed most of something
hindi: सफ़ाचट कर दिया; तबाह कर दिया
trick: DECI = tenth - Romans killed one in ten; now it means wiped out.
examples: I had just decimated a box of donuts and a chocolate shake.
The kids decimated the pizza in five minutes.

meaning: A floor or level of a building, bus or ship; also a pack of cards
trick: DECK of a ship = its floor.
examples: We lived on the second deck of an apartment complex.
We sat on the top deck of the bus.

meaning: Slowly rotting after death
trick: DE-COMPOSE = un-make; the body breaks down.
examples: Giti's decomposing right foot would be found on a rooftop two weeks later.
There was a decomposing rat under the floor.

meaning: Separated two things that were linked
trick: DE-COUPLE = no longer a couple.
examples: Once I decided it belonged to me and decoupled it from the calendar, I felt confident.
She decoupled her happiness from other people's opinions.

meaning: An official order given by a ruler or government
trick: DECREE - the king DECREES: 'it shall be!'
examples: By a special decree of Comrade Napoleon, Beasts of England had been abolished.
The king issued a decree banning the festival.

meaning: Openly refusing to obey or respect someone
trick: DEFY -> DEFIANCE: saying 'no' to power.
examples: It seemed worthwhile to endure all for this act of defiance.
In defiance of the rules, he stayed out late.

usage.pattern: an act of defiance / in defiance of something

meaning: Openly refusing to obey or showing no fear
trick: DEFIANT - you DEFY them.
examples: Nana stood with her arms crossed in a defiant and mocking way.
The boy gave a defiant look to his teacher.

meaning: In a way that shows you refuse to obey or are not afraid
trick: DEFIANT + -ly.
examples: He grinned at her defiantly.
She defiantly refused to say sorry.

meaning: Amounts by which money spent is more than money received; shortfalls
trick: DEFICIT - money is DEFICIENT (short).
examples: Self-esteem could lead to lower crime and lower budget deficits.
The country has huge budget deficits.

meaning: Went against what was expected or did not obey
trick: DEFIED expectations = flew past them.
examples: His popularity defied everyone's expectations.
The old man defied his doctors and lived to 100.

meaning: Clear and certain; not vague
trick: DEFINITE - it has a clear DEFINITion; spelled with 'ite', not 'ate'.
examples: Clover thought she remembered a definite ruling against beds.
We don't have a definite plan yet.

usage.pattern: a definite + noun / be definite about something

meaning: Feeling sad and less confident, as if the air has gone out of you
trick: DEFLATED like a balloon with the air let out.
examples: Mariam watched him leave, deflated at the thought of the long week ahead.
He felt deflated after losing the match.

meaning: To make something change direction or turn away
trick: DE-FLECT = bend away (like a shield deflects arrows).
examples: Another thing I did to deflect the course of my thoughts was to listen to my heart.
He tried to deflect the question with a joke.

meaning: To make a tense or dangerous situation calmer
trick: DE-FUSE a bomb = remove its fuse so it won't blow up.
examples: You'll learn how to defuse negative dynamics by bringing them into the open.
She told a joke to defuse the tension.

meaning: Treatment that makes someone lose respect and dignity; also damage that makes something worse
trick: DE-GRADE = drop a grade, lower yourself.
examples: It had been a place of abasement, of degradation and despair.
Prisoners lived in filth and degradation.

meaning: Sad and disappointed
trick: DE-JECTED = thrown down (like 'reject').
examples: He sank back in his chair, looking limp and dejected.
She looked dejected after failing the test.

meaning: Very pleasant; also delicious
trick: DELECTABLE - so DELIGHTful you want to eat it.
examples: How delectable it was to think of this baby, her baby.
The cake looked delectable.

meaning: Small, fine and graceful; also easily broken
trick: DELICATE like a DELI-cake - handle with care.
examples: She had a delicate chin and long, black hair.
Be careful, that glass is delicate.

meaning: Great pleasure or happiness
trick: DE-LIGHT - joy lights up your face.
examples: In these dreams, Nana cackled with delight and vindication.
The children screamed with delight.

usage.pattern: with delight / to someone's delight / a delight

meaning: The act of clearly marking the line or difference between things
trick: DE-LINE = draw a LINE between.
examples: By boundaries I mean the delineation between two people's responsibilities.
There is no clear delineation between work and home for him.

meaning: Young people who break the law or behave badly
trick: DELINQUENT - delin-QUIT school, broke rules.
examples: I hung out with gang bangers and other borderline delinquents.
The police caught a group of delinquents breaking windows.

meaning: A state of confused, wild thinking, often from illness or exhaustion
trick: DELIRIUM - your mind goes off the rails (Latin 'off the furrow').
examples: Finding laughter in the pain and delirium turned everything upside down.
The fever left him in delirium all night.

meaning: The thick triangle-shaped muscle on top of the shoulder
trick: DELTA = triangle; the DELTOID is triangle-shaped.
examples: They would aim for the muscle that Tariq called the deltoid.
The nurse gave the injection in my deltoid.

meaning: To make someone (or yourself) believe something false
trick: DELUDE -> DELUSION: living in a false world.
examples: They must constantly delude or distract themselves from reality.
Don't delude yourself that he will change.

meaning: A huge amount of something arriving at once; also a great flood
trick: DELUGE - a DELUxe-sized flood.
examples: The deluge of exceptional information drives us to feel insecure.
After the ad, we got a deluge of emails.

meaning: Believing things that are clearly not true
trick: DELUSION + -al = living in a dream.
examples: He had a delusional level of self-confidence.
She's delusional if she thinks she'll win without practice.

meaning: To look into something deeply and in detail
trick: DELVE = DIG into - like digging with a spade.
examples: We won't delve into the biology of sitting in the same spot for days.
Let's delve into the details of the plan.

meaning: The way someone looks and behaves (American spelling; British: demeanour)
trick: DEMEANOR - your 'manner'; both have 'mean' and 'or'/'er'.
examples: The brawny one, with the scornful demeanor, was the leader.
She has a calm and friendly demeanor.

meaning: The death or end of someone or something
trick: DEMISE - DE + 'mise' = the curtain falls.
examples: He struggled with it as he stared down his own demise.
The shop's demise came after the big mall opened.

usage.pattern: someone's demise / the demise of something

meaning: A public meeting or march to protest; also showing how something works
trick: DEMONSTRATE = show; a crowd SHOWS its anger.
examples: Two days later, there was a large demonstration in Kabul.
Students held a demonstration against the fee hike.

meaning: In a quiet, shy and modest way
trick: DEMURE - a quiet 'mur'mur of a smile.
examples: Nana smiled demurely when he said this.
The girl looked down demurely.

meaning: Refusing to accept that something true or painful is real; also saying something is not true
trick: DENIAL - it's not just a river in Egypt (the Nile)!
examples: Denial was the first thing she felt.
He is still in denial about his illness.

meaning: Publicly said that something or someone is wrong or evil
trick: DE-NOUNCE = announce against.
examples: Becker fell into a crowd that denounced the practice of psychiatry as a form of fascism.
The leader denounced the attack on TV.

meaning: A product that removes or hides bad smells
trick: DE-ODOR = remove the odour (smell).
examples: Each afternoon, I sprayed my stock with aerosol deodorizer.
The bathroom needs some deodorizer.

meaning: To show or describe something in a picture or words
trick: DEPICT = make a PICTure of it.
examples: Many of the drawings depict tanks running over huts.
The film depicts life in a small village.

usage.pattern: depict something / depict someone as something

meaning: Showed or described something in a picture or words
trick: DEPICTED - put in a PICTure.
examples: It depicted simply an enormous face, more than a metre wide.
The painting depicted a quiet river.

usage.pattern: depicted something / depicted someone as something

meaning: A way of showing or describing something in art, film or writing
trick: DEPICTION = the PICTure you paint.
examples: A powerful, harrowing depiction of Afghanistan.
The movie gives a true depiction of war.

meaning: Putting something down in a place; also putting money in a bank
trick: DEPOSIT = put it down (like money in a bank).
examples: Laila began moving things to the yard and depositing them by the front door.
He kept depositing his bags on the table.

meaning: Morally very bad; evil
trick: DE-PRAVED = de-PRAISED: nothing good to praise.
examples: Depraved, he called them.
Only a depraved person would hurt a child.

meaning: To take something away from someone, or stop them having it
trick: DE-PRIVE - make someone PRIVATE-ly poor.
examples: These facts seemed to deprive the court's decision of much of its gravity.
Don't deprive yourself of sleep.

meaning: Took something important away from someone
trick: DEPRIVED - left without.
examples: I've deprived your son of his father.
The war deprived many children of school.

meaning: A small group sent to speak or act for others
trick: DEPUTY -> DEPUTATION: a team of deputies.
examples: A deputation of neighbouring farmers had been invited to make a tour.
A deputation of workers met the manager.

meaning: Laughing at someone in an unkind way
trick: DERISION - deride = ride on someone with laughs.
examples: She could will herself to absorb Mariam's derision and finger-pointing.
His idea was met with derision.

meaning: The thick layer of skin under the top layer, with nerves and blood vessels
trick: DERM = skin (dermatologist = skin doctor).
examples: Both palms were filleted open down to the dermis.
The cut went deep into the dermis.

meaning: (Of a group) arrived at a place suddenly, often in large numbers; also went down
hindi: आ धमकीं, उमड़ पड़ीं; नीचे उतरे
trick: DESCEND on a place - swoop DOWN like birds.
examples: A flock of neighborhood women descended on the house.
Relatives descended on our home for the wedding.

meaning: Arrives or comes down suddenly
trick: DESCENDS - comes DOWN on you.
examples: Sometimes the unexpected descends like chaos.
Silence descends when the teacher walks in.

meaning: The act of going down, especially a slope
trick: DESCENT goes down; aSCENT goes up.
examples: Each lap demanded an ascent and descent of around 5,000 vertical feet.
The plane began its descent into Delhi.

meaning: Making someone less sensitive or less upset by something through repeated exposure
trick: DE-SENSITIVE = taking the sensitivity away.
examples: The teenagers set out on intensive desensitization exercises.
Desensitization helped her lose her fear of dogs.

meaning: Left empty; no one there anymore
trick: DESERTED like a DESERT - nobody around.
examples: There is a deserted bird's nest in one corner.
The streets were deserted at midnight.

meaning: Large, dry areas of land with very little rain and few plants
trick: DESERTS have one S (sand); DESSERTS have two S (sweet stuff).
examples: She was separated from the life she'd known by valleys, mountains and entire deserts.
Camels can walk across deserts for days without water.

usage.pattern: cross deserts / across the deserts of somewhere

meaning: The feeling or state of having earned or being worthy of something
trick: DESERVE + D + NESS: the state of believing you DESERVE it.
examples: They must feel certain of their own beliefs and deservedness.
His sense of deservedness made him expect a reward for everything.

usage.pattern: a sense of deservedness / someone's deservedness

meaning: Things that are wanted or needed (plural of desideratum); here, a person's treasured bits and pieces
trick: DESIRE → DESIderata: the things you DESIRE.
examples: Each box is loaded with its own silly teen desiderata—colored pens, old notes and CDs.
A quiet room and good light are my desiderata for studying.

meaning: Very sad and lonely; also (of a place) empty and bleak
trick: DESOLATE = DE-SOLO: left all SOLO and sad.
examples: Babi sat alone on a folding chair in the hallway, looking desolate and small.
She felt desolate after her best friend moved away.

usage.pattern: look / feel desolate; a desolate + place

meaning: The complete loss of hope
trick: DE-SPAIR: no SPARE hope left.
examples: I explained that it wasn't despair I felt, but fear.
He cried out in despair when he failed the exam again.

meaning: Deserving hatred and contempt; very bad
trick: DESPICABLE sounds like 'Despicable Me': the villain you love to hate.
examples: "You're despicable," Laila said.
Cheating a poor old man is a despicable thing to do.

meaning: In a way that shows strong dislike or looking down on someone
trick: DESPISE + -INGLY: looking at someone as if you DESPISE them.
examples: He did not look at Mariam despisingly.
The rich man looked despisingly at the beggar.

meaning: Sad and without hope
trick: DESPONDENT: your hopes have DESPONDed (gone down) the drain.
examples: He cast a despondent glance toward Mariam, then his mother.
She was despondent after losing her job.

meaning: The state of being kept in a prison or similar place; also a punishment of staying late at school
trick: DETENTION: they DETAIN you and don't let you go.
examples: He landed in a youth detention center for six months.
The boy got detention for talking in class.

meaning: Becomes worse over time
trick: DETERIORATES: things go DETERIOR... down the stairs, getting worse each step.
examples: It is a marriage that soon deteriorates into brutality and misery.
His health deteriorates every winter.

meaning: To decide or judge something; also to find out a fact exactly
trick: DETERMINE: you TERMINATE the doubt by deciding.
examples: They tried to determine whether things had been better or worse than now.
The doctor will determine what is wrong with you.

meaning: To hate something or someone very much
trick: DE-TEST: you DETEST a surprise TEST.
examples: Though so much alike, they detest each other.
I detest waking up early on Sundays.

meaning: A longer way around, taken to avoid something or for a reason; also a break from the usual path
trick: DE-TOUR: a little TOUR off the main road.
examples: Napoleon's dogs made a detour under cover of the hedge.
The road was closed, so we took a detour through the village.

meaning: To think up or invent a plan or method
trick: DEVISE a DEVICE: you plan it before you build it.
examples: Have you ever tried to devise a win-win solution with a guy who thinks he's the messiah?
We need to devise a way to save more money.

usage.pattern: devise a plan / way / method (to do something)

meaning: Thinking up or inventing a plan or scheme
hindi: योजना बनाते हुए, साज़िश रचते हुए
trick: DEVISING: working on a secret DEVICE in your head.
examples: They sat in the shoe shop all day, devising secret plots.
The kids were devising a plan to surprise their mother.

meaning: Entirely without something
trick: DEVOID = a VOID: totally empty of something.
examples: It was a life devoid of any drive and passion.
The room was devoid of furniture.

meaning: Ate something quickly and hungrily; also read or enjoyed eagerly
trick: DEVOURED: the hungry DEVIL ate everything in an hour.
examples: Sheep broke down hedges and devoured the clover.
The kids devoured the pizza in five minutes.

meaning: Very religious and faithful
trick: DEVOUT people make a VOW to God.
examples: Najibullah tried to portray himself as a devout Muslim.
My grandmother is devout and prays every morning.

meaning: Tiny drops of water that form on grass and leaves overnight
trick: DEW is DUE every morning on the grass.
examples: They rolled in the dew and cropped mouthfuls of sweet summer grass.
The grass was wet with dew in the morning.

usage.pattern: wet with dew / the morning dew

meaning: A form of a language spoken in one area or by one group
trick: DIALECT: how people DIAL (speak) in their own area.
examples: She was unaccustomed to the Kabuli dialect of his Farsi.
My grandparents speak a village dialect of Hindi.

usage.pattern: speak a dialect / the dialect of a place

meaning: (with 'in') Set something up exactly right; also pressed numbers to make a phone call
hindi: सटीक रूप से सेट किया; नंबर मिलाया
trick: Like turning a DIAL until the setting is perfect.
examples: Most athletes were self-reliant and dialed in their own nutrition plan.
She dialed in her camera settings before the shoot.

usage.pattern: dial in something / have something dialed in

meaning: To control or decide what happens; also to say words for someone to write down
hindi: तय करना, नियंत्रित करना; बोलकर लिखवाना
trick: A DICTATOR DICTATES everything.
examples: I was a quitter who had let fear dictate my future.
Don't let other people dictate how you live.

meaning: Changed into a digital form for use on a computer
trick: DIGIT-ized: turned into DIGITS (0s and 1s).
examples: The test had been digitized and I wasn't experienced with computers.
The old family photos were digitized.

meaning: (of a building or thing) Old and in very bad condition
trick: DILAPIDATED: the LAPIS (stone) is falling off the walls.
examples: Men with pickaxes swarmed the dilapidated Kabul Museum.
They lived in a dilapidated old house.

meaning: Becomes wider or larger; here, time seems to stretch out
trick: DILATES: the eye doctor DILATES your pupils to make them wide.
examples: Time extends itself and dilates, so seconds feel like eons.
The pupil dilates in the dark.

meaning: Careful and steady effort; ('due ...') the careful checking expected before a decision
trick: DILIGENCE: DILIGENT people DIG until it's done.
examples: If you're doing your post-faceplant due diligence, you should do that too.
She passed the exam through hard work and diligence.

usage.pattern: with diligence / do your due diligence

meaning: With careful, steady and hard effort
trick: DILIGENTLY: DIG-it-GENTLY but keep digging all day.
examples: They worked diligently, hardly raising their faces from the ground.
She diligently did her homework every evening.

meaning: (of memories) Not clear, hard to remember; also not bright
trick: DIM the lights: everything gets hard to see.
examples: The older animals racked their dim memories.
I have only a dim memory of my first school.

meaning: A US coin worth ten cents; ('every ...') all of someone's money
trick: DIME = a tiny coin; 'not a dime' = not a paisa.
examples: "You got literally every dime he had," she said.
He doesn't have a dime to his name.

meaning: Becoming smaller or less; ('... returns') less benefit for each extra effort
trick: DIMINISHING: MINI-shing, getting MINI-er.
examples: There are diminishing returns to each new adventure.
Our water supply is diminishing fast.

meaning: A loud, unpleasant, continuous noise
trick: DIN sounds like 'DIN-DIN-DIN': a noisy racket.
examples: A big truck came up with a din of chains and backfires.
We couldn't hear each other over the din of the traffic.

usage.pattern: the din of something / over the din

meaning: Dark, dull and dirty-looking
trick: DINGY: DIrty + duNGY.
examples: Laila lay on a bed inside the old, dingy operating room.

examples: The drought, started in 1998, was wreaking havoc everywhere.
Farmers lost their crops in the drought.

usage.pattern: a drought hits a place / suffer from drought

meaning: The state of feeling sleepy and heavy
trick: DROWSY = DROWNing in sleep.
examples: Then came the drowsiness and the frightening disorientation.
This medicine may cause drowsiness.

meaning: Sleepy and slow, nearly falling asleep; also making things quiet and sleepy
trick: DROWSY = DROWNing in sleep.
examples: She noticed a drowsy hush overtaking Kabul.
I felt drowsy after a big lunch.

usage.pattern: feel / get drowsy / a drowsy + noun

meaning: Hard, boring work that must be done again and again
trick: DRUDGERY: you DRAG yourself through it.
examples: Laila remembered the inescapable drudgery of those four weeks without Tariq.
Washing dishes every night felt like drudgery.

usage.pattern: the drudgery of something / of doing something

meaning: Tapping something again and again with the fingers, like on a drum
trick: Fingers DRUMMING = playing the table like a DRUM.
examples: Rasheed was drumming his gloved fingers and humming a song.
She sat drumming her fingers on the table.

meaning: Not seeming honest or trustworthy; also unsure or doubtful
trick: DUBIOUS = DOUBT-ious: full of doubt.
examples: He was a man of more than dubious reputation.
I'm dubious about his story.

usage.pattern: a dubious + noun / be dubious about something

meaning: To avoid something difficult; also to lower your head or body quickly to avoid being hit
trick: DUCK your head like a DUCK diving under water.
examples: To duck our problems is to lead a meaningless existence.
He ducked when the ball flew at him.

usage.pattern: duck something / duck out of something

meaning: Young baby ducks
trick: DUCK + LING (little) = little ducks.
examples: A brood of ducklings, which had lost their mother, filed into the barn.
The ducklings followed their mother to the pond.

meaning: Strong, wide, silver sticky tape used for quick repairs
trick: It was made to seal air DUCTS (pipes).
examples: Buried beneath my dive gear were two rolls of duct tape.
He fixed the broken chair with duct tape.

usage.pattern: a roll of duct tape / duct-tape something

meaning: Opposing each other, fighting for control (of feelings or ideas); also fighting a duel
trick: Two feelings in a DUEL, like two swordsmen.
examples: Mammy was soon asleep, leaving Laila with dueling emotions.
The two shops ran dueling ads on TV.

meaning: Searched through something with your hands; also pushed into, or made a hole (past of dig)
trick: DIG → DUG: you dig through a bag like digging soil.
examples: I dug through my dive bag.
She dug through her purse for her keys.

meaning: Canoes made by hollowing out a tree trunk; also shelters dug in the ground
trick: A log DUG OUT inside = a DUGOUT canoe.
examples: We slept in hammocks and paddled dugouts through the jungle.
The villagers crossed the river in dugouts.

usage.pattern: paddle dugouts / travel in a dugout

meaning: In the right or expected way; at the expected time
trick: DULY = DUE-ly: done as it is DUE.
examples: Our nervous system duly punishes us to make sure we pay attention.
The form was duly signed and sent.

meaning: So surprised that you cannot speak
trick: DUMB (can't speak) + FOUNDED = struck dumb.
examples: Mariam was dumbfounded that she could miss a being she had never seen.
We were dumbfounded by the news.

meaning: A large metal container for rubbish (American)
trick: DUMP your trash in the DUMPSTER.
examples: I slammed the dumpster shut.
He threw the old sofa in the dumpster.

meaning: Hills of sand made by the wind, in deserts or near the sea
trick: DUNES of sand, like in the desert film 'Dune'.
examples: The dunes stretched as far as we could see.
We rode camels over the sand dunes in Jaisalmer.

meaning: Solid waste from animals, often used as fertilizer or fuel
trick: Cow DUNG = gobar.
examples: Our labour tills the soil, our dung fertilises it.
Villagers use cow dung as fuel.

meaning: Trousers with a bib and straps over the shoulders, often of denim; also work trousers
trick: DUNGAREES got their name from DONGRI in Mumbai, where the cloth was made.
examples: I noticed two Arabs in blue dungarees coming in our direction.
The painter wore old dungarees.

meaning: A dark underground room or prison, as in a castle
trick: DUNGEON = DUNG + EON: stuck in a smelly dark room for ages.
examples: That meant losing the glitz and setting up shop in a dungeon.
The king threw the thief into the dungeon.

usage.pattern: in a dungeon / throw someone into a dungeon

meaning: Tricked into believing something false
trick: DUPED = made a DUMMY of.
examples: I'd duped myself into a loop of cheating that looked like progress.
Many people were duped by the fake lottery call.

usage.pattern: dupe someone into doing something / be duped by someone

meaning: The time in the evening just before it gets dark
trick: DUSK is DUSKY (darkish): dawn → dusk.
examples: The winds would blow from midmorning to dusk.
The street lights come on at dusk.

usage.pattern: at dusk / from dawn to dusk

meaning: Fine dry powder of earth or dirt
trick: DUST sounds a bit like Hindi 'dhool'.
examples: He would trace out A, B, C, D in the dust with his great hoof.
The old books were covered in dust.

usage.pattern: in the dust / covered in dust

meaning: In an obedient way, doing what you are expected to do
trick: DUTY-FULLY: doing your DUTY fully.
examples: Mariam would listen dutifully to this.
The children dutifully cleaned their rooms.

meaning: Made something seem small or unimportant by being much bigger
hindi: छोटा कर दिया, फीका कर दिया
trick: Next to a giant you look like a DWARF — you are DWARFED.
examples: Her love for it already dwarfed anything she had ever felt.
The tall tower dwarfed the houses around it.

usage.pattern: dwarf something / be dwarfed by something

meaning: Makes something seem small by being much bigger; also (plural noun) very short people or creatures in stories
trick: Next to a giant you look like a DWARF.
examples: It explodes into a fireball that dwarfs any ball of fire Laila has ever seen.
The new mall dwarfs the old shops nearby.

meaning: To keep thinking or talking about something, usually bad (used with 'on'); also to live somewhere
trick: DWELL = staying down in a WELL of thoughts too long.
examples: There was no time to dwell on fear.
Don't dwell on your mistakes; learn from them.

usage.pattern: dwell on something / dwell in a place

meaning: Coloured with a special liquid
trick: DYED (colour) vs DIED (death): the Y is for colour.
examples: He carried a basket of dyed eggs for Mariam.
She dyed her hair red.

meaning: Machines that turn movement into electricity; also (singular, informal) very energetic people
trick: Greek 'dynamis' = power, like DYNAMite.
examples: After the sails, there would be need for dynamos and cables.
Old bicycles had dynamos to power their lights.

meaning: A serious gut infection causing severe diarrhoea, often with blood
trick: DYS (bad) + ENTERY (intestines, as in 'gastro-entero'): bad guts.
examples: Then there was dysentery, feared with every loose stool.
Dirty water can give you dysentery.

meaning: A state of not working normally or healthily, in a body, mind or group
trick: DYS (bad) + FUNCTION = working badly.
examples: Denying negative emotions leads to emotional dysfunction.
The family's dysfunction was hard on the kids.
